<meta>continues from previous page: the simile of the lotus pond, illustrating the third meditative absorption</meta>
132 Long Discourses <note>original: "Dīghanikāya"</note>, The Division on Morality <note>original: "Sīlakkhandhavagga"</note>, The Discourse on the Fruits of the Recluse's Life <note>original: "Sāmaññaphalasutta"</note>

In just the same way, great king, a monk drenches, steeps, fills and pervades this very body with a happiness free of rapture, so that there is no part of his whole body that is not suffused with that happiness free of rapture. <note>The printed form reads "tipatitakena", which appears to be a misreading of "nippītikena", "free of rapture", the standard phrase for the third absorption.</note>

This too, great king, is a fruit of the recluse's life visible here and now, more excellent and more sublime than the visible fruits of the recluse's life described before.

68. And further, great king, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the earlier disappearance of joy and sorrow, a monk enters and dwells in the fourth <term>jhāna</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss>, which is neither painful nor pleasant and has a purity of mindfulness born of equanimity. He sits pervading this very body with a pure, bright mind, so that there is no part of his whole body that is not suffused with that pure, bright mind.

Just as, great king, a man might sit wrapped from head to foot in a white cloth, so that there would be no part of his whole body not covered by the white cloth; in just the same way, great king, a monk sits pervading this very body with a pure, bright mind, so that there is no part of his whole body that is not suffused with that pure, bright mind.

This too, great king, is a fruit of the recluse's life visible here and now, more excellent and more sublime than the visible fruits of the recluse's life described before.

69. And further, great king, when his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, supple, workable, steady and attained to imperturbability, that monk directs and inclines his mind. <note>In the standard text the mind is directed "to knowledge and vision" (ñāṇadassanāya); that phrase does not appear in the printed text on this page.</note> He understands thus: "This body of mine has form; it is made of the four great elements, born of mother and father, built up out of rice and porridge, and is subject to impermanence, to rubbing and pressing, to breaking up and dispersal. And this consciousness <note>original: "viññāṇa"</note> of mine is supported here and bound up here."

70. Just as, great king, there might be a beautiful beryl gem <note>original: "maṇi veḷuriyo"</note> of the finest water, eight-faceted, well cut, clear, translucent, flawless, perfect in every respect, and through it a thread is strung, blue or yellow or red or white or brown. A man with good eyes, taking it in his hand, would examine it: "This is a beautiful beryl gem of the finest water, eight-faceted, well cut, clear, translucent, flawless, perfect in every respect; and through it a thread is strung, blue or yellow or red or white or brown."

<summary>King Ajātasattu is told of the further fruits of the recluse's life: the happiness of the third absorption and the pure, bright awareness of the fourth, each illustrated by a simile. The monk then turns his concentrated mind to insight, seeing the body as impermanent and consciousness as bound to it, illustrated by the simile of a thread seen through a clear beryl gem.</summary>
